newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda says it expects genocide trials to pick up.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda says it expects genocide trials to pick up.

text.p: Rwanda's justice ministry said on Thursday it expected a trickle of trials since December of suspects involved in the 1994 genocide to pick up as courts gain experience.
Gerard Gahima, head of cabinet at the justice ministry, said prosecutors who concentrated on preparing for the first trials in December had not planned ahead to keep up the momentum.

"We have arrived at some kind of slowdown, but I expect things to proceed and pick up," Gahima told Reuters. "If you have thousands of cases in your jurisdiction it is not very difficult at all to take a case a day or several cases a day."
State radio said on Thursday a tribunal in Cyangugu in the southwest had found guilty and sentenced a suspect to death, bringing the total death sentences so far to at least 11.
Sixteen people have been sentenced to life imprisonment and only one of the accused to appear so far has been acquitted.

Those who have appeared before special tribunals so far are a tiny proportion of the more than 90,000 suspects crammed into Rwanda's jails and lockups accused of involvement in the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

Under a genocide law passed in 1996, ringleaders of the genocide and those who committed particularly horrific crimes receive the mandatory death sentence. Investigations have led to a list of 1,946 such people but some are not yet in custody.
In three lesser categories, the death sentence is not automatic and penalties can be cut in return for confessions.
But few accused have confessed and no confessions have been accepted in court. Two were rejected after the accused failed to name their accomplices.
Those sentenced to death have 15 days to appeal against sentence and the courts have three months to accept an appeal.
Officials therefore say it could be several months before any executions of genocide killers are carried out, which according to law are by firing squad and away from public view.
"We are not in a hurry to put anybody to death, it must first be established whether they are guilty," Gahima said.
The most important Rwandan so far sentenced to death is Froduald Karamira, a Tutsi who became a Hutu by a traditional practice and appealed by radio for people to kill neighbours.
Rwanda is critical of a parallel U.N. genocide tribunal with its headquarters in Arusha, Tanzania, and complains it is slow, has failed to investigate crimes fully and is badly organised.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan dismissed two top officials of the U.N. tribunal following a U.N. investigation that found widespread mismanagement and financial waste.
They were the deputy prosecutor, Honoure Rakotomanana, a judge from Madagascar, and the registrar, Andonico Adede of Kenya, who in effect served as tribunal chief administrator.
The tribunal has so far indicted a total of 21 people.
